content_html_sanitized:
Posted July 18, 2004
Analysis by Richard Cowan Sponsored By Advanced Nutrients.

On June 29th, I wrote about the embarrassment for the marijuana reform movement caused by the Marijuana Policy Projects incompetence in pushing an initiative in Nevada.
See
Richard Lee's Oakland Initiative To Be On November Ballot, But MPP's Nevada Initiative May Not Make It, And IT SHOULD NOT! Fiasco Embarrasses and Undermines Cannabis Movement With Mandatory Minimums!

They forgot to turn in thousands of signatures from Clark County (Las Vegas). Of course, this has brought ridicule to the movement because it plays to the stereotype of the absent-minded stoner. It is ironic and even more outrageous that this fiasco was perpetrated by an organization that has done everything possible to distance itself from the cannabis community.

Just as he has equivocated about his own marijuana use, Rob Kampia has repeatedly equivocated about whether MPP really supports the legalization of marijuana. Even its motto Minimize the harm associated with marijuana is ambiguous. A nark could certainly sign on to that.

It now seems certain that having wasted hundreds of thousands of dollars of Peter Lewis money the proposed amendment to the Nevada constitution will not be on the November ballot.

Incredibly, this is actually good news for reformers. Because MPP under Kampia refuses to consult with anyone else in the marijuana reform movement, and will not work with local activists, the Nevada initiative contained provisions that most activists simply could not support.

(For example, it would add to the constitution a provision that would Establish a penalty of one to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000 for a person who has attained the age of 18 years who does not own or work at an establishment that is licensed to sell marijuana who is convicted of a first offense of distributing or selling marijuana to a minor, and a maximum penalty of life in prison for a second or subsequent offense of distributing or selling marijuana to a minor. As I pointed out, an 18 year-old college student who buys weed for his friends would have to go to prison for at least a year!)

However, the news from Arkansas is even stranger. There they are abandoning an effort to get a medical marijuana initiative on the November ballot, even though there seems to be a very good chance of succeeding.

MPP claims that the reason are pulling the plug is that they have discovered that there is a Presidential election this year and two unknown groups called Democrats and Republicans are buying lots of advertising, so it would cost too much to buy ads for an initiative that is supported by an overwhelming majority of the people.

Mind you, this is the same group that failed to notice that their last attempt in Nevada would be complicated by the presence of an anti-gay marriage amendment on the ballot in a state with a large Mormon population.
From 2002 see
I m A Legalizer. What Are You? The Nevada Fiasco. Analysis by Richard Cowan

Although the front page of the MPP website has six pictures of Rob Kampia, there is no mention of the Arkansas mess. My sources tell me that the real reason that MPP pulled out was because they had so alienated the local activists that it was about to blow up in their faces.

This is typical of the MPP modus operandi. In Washington, DC, the local Act-Up (AIDS activist) organization had already passed a medical marijuana initiative without any help from the Billionaires Boys Club.
See
Court Orders DC Medical Marijuana Vote Count Released And The Initiative Wins With 69%!

However, MPP decided to promote another initiative of their own so that they could take credit for it and get maximum media coverage. In a familiar pattern, the MPP initiative never made it on the ballot despite spending hundreds of thousands of Peter Lewis money. (Although Lewis is by far the largest supporter of MPP, they also use Lewis money to con others far less wealthy into supporting them.)

To make matters even more outrageous, MPP actually ended up in litigation with ACT-UP, so what happened in Arkansas comes as no surprise. Meanwhile the Arkansas activists, Arkansas Alliance for Medical Marijuana, the people who actually live there, are continuing to work to get the initiative on the ballot, and they may yet succeed.

For more on the story see Phil Smith's excellent article:
MPP Pulls Out Of Arkansas Medical Marijuana Initiative Campaign

In contrast, Oregon and Alaska will have initiatives on the ballot in November. MPP refused to help the local activists because they would have had to share the credit with the people who live on the front lines. These are the people who really need and deserve our support.

This story is far from over, and in the next few weeks we will learn more. Perhaps we will learn if Peter Lewis will continue to support Kampia's war on the real activists in the cannabis communities. George Soros has acknowledged that occasionally some of his truly vast philanthropies have been counterproductive. One hopes that Lewis will not abandon his support for ending cannabis prohibition, but will listen to people like Dr. Lester Grinspoon instead.

Similarly, I hope that the cannabis community will realize that NORML and the groups in Alaska and Oregon need our support now more than ever.

We must not only fight to end prohibition, we must also fight to take back our movement from the opportunists who pay themselves huge salaries and refuse to release the legally required info about their finances. (MPP redacts the part showing how much Kampia makes.)

Ultimately, the problem is not what Kampia and Lewis are doing. The real problem is what millions of other cannabis users are not doing to defend their own freedom.
